p: Since a big top-to-bottom redevelopment, the museum has been laid out around five main galleries, each looking at the Army from a different angle: the soldiers themselves, the Army as an organisation, the battles it fought, the way it touches everyday society, and the wider questions it raises. That makes it easier to dip in than you might expect, because you can head straight for whichever theme grabs you rather than marching chronologically through four hundred years.

One object that stops people in their tracks is the skeleton of Marengo, the horse Napoleon is said to have ridden at Waterloo. It's a strange, oddly moving thing to stand next to, and it tends to spark plenty of questions from younger visitors. Elsewhere you'll find uniforms you can compare across the centuries, letters home, paintings and the kind of small personal items that make a big story feel close.

General admission is free, which takes the pressure off. A couple of hours is about right for most people, though anyone tracing a grandparent's regiment could easily stay longer. If that's you, jot down whatever you already know, such as names, service numbers and regiments, before you go, as it makes the displays far more meaningful. Smaller children have their own play space aimed at the under-eights, handy for burning off energy between galleries.

Royal Hospital Road is a lovely street to linger on. The Chelsea Physic Garden is a few minutes' walk along the same road, the grounds of the Royal Hospital host the famous flower show each May, and crossing Chelsea Bridge brings you into Battersea Park for a run around by the river.
